month.title: Auth + security + reliability
month.theme: Make the app safe for more than one person, and less fragile when things go wrong.
month.mastery: Threat-model the application and identify major failure points.
month.checkpoint: A multi-user app where users can only see their own data, with a written threat model and tested failure paths.

weeks.title: Authentication
weeks.objective: Let people prove who they are, using proven providers rather than home-made password code.
learn: Authentication vs authorization
Sessions vs tokens (cookies, JWTs)
Passwords, hashing, and why you shouldn't roll your own
OAuth and 'Sign in with Google', conceptually
Magic links and passkeys
Managed auth providers (Supabase Auth, Auth.js, Clerk)
Protecting routes on the server
practice: Draw the sign-in flow for a magic link, step by step
Inspect the cookies set when you log in to a site you use
Add sign-in to a throwaway app with a managed provider
Visit a protected page while logged out and confirm the server blocks it

build.title: Sign-in for the client tracker
build.brief: Add authentication to your client tracker using a managed provider. Protected routes redirect to sign-in, sign-out works, and sessions survive a refresh.

weeks.prove: Explain what is stored where (browser, server, provider) after sign-in, and what happens on sign-out.
reflect: What did the auth provider do that you would never have thought to build?
weeks.ship: Deployed app with working sign-in and sign-out.

tryFirst.task: A page /dashboard should only render for signed-in users. Where must that check happen, and why isn't hiding the link enough?
tryFirst.hint: Anything in the browser can be bypassed by typing a URL or calling the API directly.
tryFirst.explanation: UI checks are for convenience; server checks are for security. Check the session on the server before rendering or returning data, and redirect if there is no session.

weeks.title: Authorization
weeks.objective: Make sure every user can only see and change what they're allowed to, enforced where it can't be bypassed.
learn: Ownership: every row belongs to someone
Checking permissions on every read and write
Roles (owner, member, viewer)
Row Level Security in Postgres
Insecure direct object references (changing an id in the URL)
Least privilege for keys and services
Testing authorization with two accounts
practice: Create two accounts and try to read user B's record as user A
Write an RLS policy that restricts rows to their owner
Add a 'viewer' role that can read but not edit
List every endpoint and who should be allowed to call it

build.title: Multi-user client tracker
build.brief: Each user sees only their own clients and projects, and a project can be shared with a 'viewer'. Enforce it in the database (RLS) or on every server query.

weeks.prove: Two-browser test: document 5 attempts to access the other user's data and show each one failing.
reflect: Which endpoint did you forget to protect at first?
weeks.ship: A permissions table (who can do what) in the README, and the deployed app.

tryFirst.task: Write a rule so users can only select their own projects (projects.owner_id = the signed-in user).
tryFirst.hint: Postgres can attach a policy to a table that filters every query automatically. Supabase exposes the current user's id via auth.uid().
tryFirst.explanation: Row Level Security applies the rule inside the database, so even a buggy query or a direct API call can't return another user's rows.

weeks.title: Security fundamentals
weeks.objective: Think like an attacker for an afternoon so your users don't have to.
learn: The OWASP Top 10 at a working level
XSS: why you never render untrusted HTML
CSRF and SameSite cookies
Secrets management: environment variables, rotation, never in git
Dependency risk: npm audit, lockfiles
Security headers (Content Security Policy basics)
Rate limiting and abuse
practice: Try an XSS payload in every text field of your app
Search your git history for leaked secrets, and rotate any you find
Run npm audit and decide what actually matters
Check your site's response headers with securityheaders.com

build.title: Security pass
build.brief: Run a structured security review of your client tracker against the OWASP Top 10. Fix the top issues, add rate limiting to sign-in and write endpoints, and document what you checked.

weeks.prove: Write a one-page security review: what you tested, what you found, what you fixed, and what remains.
reflect: What would an attacker find first in your app?
weeks.ship: SECURITY.md in the repo, with the fixes merged.

tryFirst.task: A comment field shows user text on a page. Someone submits: . What happens with plain innerHTML vs React, and what's the rule?
tryFirst.hint: One of these treats text as text. The other treats text as code.
tryFirst.explanation: innerHTML parses the string as HTML, so the onerror handler runs (XSS). React escapes text by default; the danger only returns if you use dangerouslySetInnerHTML. The rule: render untrusted input as text, and sanitise it if you truly need HTML.

weeks.title: Error handling, validation and reliability
weeks.objective: Design for failure: validate everything, fail visibly and recover gracefully.
learn: Validation on the client (for UX) and on the server (for truth)
Error boundaries and user-facing error messages
Timeouts, retries with backoff, and idempotency keys
Logging and error monitoring (for example Sentry)
Graceful degradation when a dependency is down
Backups and restore
Writing a runbook
practice: Simulate a slow and a failing database call, and see what the user sees
Add a timeout and a bounded retry to one external call
Make 'create invoice' safe to retry with an idempotency key
Add error monitoring and trigger a test error

build.title: Reliability pass
build.brief: Make the client tracker resilient: error boundaries, consistent error responses, timeouts and retries on external calls, error monitoring, and a restore-from-backup test.

weeks.prove: Mastery test: threat-model the application and identify its major failure points.
reflect: Which failure would have lost a user's data before this week?
weeks.ship: A runbook (RUNBOOK.md), the threat model, and the deployed resilient app.

tryFirst.task: A 'Create invoice' button sometimes gets clicked twice on slow connections and creates duplicate invoices. Fix it properly.
tryFirst.hint: Disabling the button helps, but the server is the source of truth. How could the server recognise the same request arriving twice?
tryFirst.explanation: Use an idempotency key: the client generates a unique key per intended action and sends it, and the server stores it with the result, so a repeat returns the same result instead of creating a duplicate. Disable the button as well, for UX rather than correctness.

mastery.title: Threat-model your application
mastery.challenge: Produce a threat model for your multi-user app: what you're protecting, who might attack or break it, how, and what you've done about it. Then prove that three of the defences work.
constraints: Use your own deployed app, not a hypothetical one
Use a simple framework (STRIDE, or assets, threats and mitigations)
Demonstrate rather than assert: each defence you claim needs evidence
criteria: Lists assets (data, accounts, secrets) and trust boundaries on a diagram
Identifies at least 8 threats or failure points, ranked by likelihood × impact
Shows three defences working (e.g. cross-user access blocked, XSS escaped, rate limit triggered)
Names the top residual risks you haven't fixed, and why
Includes failure points that aren't attacks (outages, bad data, double submits)
A non-security person can follow it
